title: Awake among the sleeping
theme: The person who stays awake among the sleeping, shaping desire after desire, is the bright, Brahman, the immortal, in which all worlds rest.

words.gram: past passive participle, m. loc. pl.
words.context: Śaṅkara: «सुप्तेषु प्राणादिषु», while the breaths and senses sleep; Raṅgarāmānuja: «सर्वेषु सुप्तेषु जीवेषु»; Madhva: when beings sleep, as in dissolution

words.role: object of nirmimāṇaḥ (first of a repeated pair)
words.context: Śaṅkara: each desired thing, «तं तमभिप्रेतं»; Raṅgarāmānuja: an absolutive, ‘having willed’, «णमुलन्तमिदम्»

words.role: subject, in apposition to yaḥ eṣaḥ

words.gram: present participle middle, m. nom. sg.
past passive participle, m. nom. pl.

sandhi.type: aḥ before a vowel other than a
sandhi.rule: After a the visarga becomes y, P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि), which is dropped, P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य), leaving the vowels apart.
The nominative ending of eṣaḥ is dropped before a consonant, P. 6.1.132 (एतत्तदोः सुलोपोऽकोरनञ्समासे हलि).
-aḥ becomes -o before a voiced consonant, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च).
A final t becomes d before a voiced sound, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते).

sandhi.type: t before a vowel; a + a
sandhi.rule: The t becomes d, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते); eva and amṛtam merge into the long vowel, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः).
A final n before l becomes a nasalised l, P. 8.4.60 (तोर्लि), written with anusvāra (or candrabindu) and ll.
Two like vowels merge into the long vowel, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः).

morphology.note: The doubled kāmaṃ kāmam expresses ‘desire after desire’. Śaṅkara reads kāma as a noun, each desired thing, the object of nirmimāṇaḥ. Raṅgarāmānuja reads it as an absolutive in -am (ṇamul), ‘having willed again and again’, the form of repeated action, P. 3.4.22 (आभीक्ष्ण्ये णमुल् च), and rejects taking kāma as the sons and other objects of desire offered at 1.1.25.
nir-√mā, ‘measure out, fashion’, with the reduplicated present (mimīte) and the middle participle -āna; the n is retroflex after the r of nir.
The locative of tad; before lokāḥ its n becomes a nasalised l (तस्मिंल्लोकाः).

translation.literal: This person who is awake among the sleeping, fashioning desire after desire — that alone is the bright, that is Brahman, that alone is called the immortal. In it all the worlds rest; no one indeed goes beyond it. This truly is that.
translation.readable: The one who stays awake while all else sleeps, shaping one wish after another — that is the bright, that is Brahman, that is called the immortal. All the worlds rest in it, and no one goes beyond it. This is that.

anvaya: यः एषः पुरुषः सुप्तेषु कामम् कामम् निर्मिमाणः जागर्ति तत् एव शुक्रम् तत् ब्रह्म तत् एव अमृतम् उच्यते । तस्मिन् सर्वे लोकाः श्रिताः । तत् उ कश्चन न अत्येति । एतत् वै तत् ।
syntax: A relative clause (yaḥ eṣa … puruṣo nirmimāṇaḥ) is taken up by the neuter tat of the main clauses: tad eva śukraṃ, tad brahma, tad evāmṛtam ucyate. The neuter tat refers to the masculine puruṣa as the reality named. Two further clauses (tasmiṃl lokāḥ śritāḥ; tad u nātyeti kaścana) repeat 2.1.9 and look ahead to 2.3.1.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: the breaths and senses, which sleep while the self keeps fashioning objects in dream, «सुप्तेषु प्राणादिषु जागर्ति न स्वपिति». Raṅgarāmānuja: all individual selves, «सर्वेषु सुप्तेषु जीवेषु». Madhva: beings asleep in dissolution, while Viṣṇu is awake.

Desired objects, fashioned by ignorance (Śaṅkara, «स्त्र्याद्यर्थमविद्यया»), or the absolutive ‘having willed again and again’ of the Lord who creates by his will (Raṅgarāmānuja). See the morphology note.

The base reads ya eṣa supteṣu, ‘he who among the sleeping’, on which Śaṅkara comments. Madhva’s text reads ya eṣu supteṣu, ‘who among these sleeping ones’ (corrections.json), as does the mūla printed with Raṅgarāmānuja.

metre.name: irregular
metre.note: Counted as written, 20, 16, 16 and 4 syllables. The first line is a long line of 9 + 11 (ya eṣa supteṣu jāgarti, then the triṣṭubh-length kāmaṃ kāmaṃ puruṣo nirmimāṇaḥ); two regular anuṣṭubh half-lines follow, and the refrain (4) stands outside the metre.

beginner: Here Death begins to tell the secret he promised. When we sleep, our senses go quiet, yet something goes on: in dreams scene after scene is made, one wish after another taking shape. Who makes them? The one who stays awake when everything else sleeps. That, says the verse, is the bright, the immortal, Brahman itself; all the worlds rest in it and nothing goes beyond it. Śaṅkara reads the sleepers as the senses and the wakeful one as the self that fashions dream objects. Raṅgarāmānuja reads it as the Lord, awake while all individual souls sleep, creating by his will. Madhva too reads it as Viṣṇu, awake when beings sleep in dissolution.
analogy: Like the one person in a dark house who stays awake through the night and sees the dreams of every sleeper.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: The person awake among the sleeping, fashioning desire after desire, is the bright, is Brahman, is called the immortal; all worlds rest in it and none goes beyond it. This is that.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: This is the secret Brahman promised in 2.2.6, «यत्प्रतिज्ञातं गुह्यं ब्रह्म प्रवक्ष्यामीति तदाह». While the breaths and senses sleep, he stays awake, fashioning each desired object through ignorance, «कामं कामं तं तमभिप्रेतं स्त्र्याद्यर्थमविद्यया निर्मिमाणः». That alone is the bright and pure, and there is no other secret Brahman, «तदेव शुक्रं शुभ्रं शुद्धं तद्ब्रह्म नान्यद्गुह्यं ब्रह्मास्ति». The last line is as at 2.1.9, «तदु नात्येति कश्चनेत्यादि पूर्ववदेव».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: While all selves sleep, «सर्वेषु सुप्तेषु जीवेषु», the Supreme creates by willing again and again, «संकल्प्य संकल्प्य स्वच्छन्दानुरोधेन»; he refers for this sense to the Bhāṣya on the Sandhya-adhikaraṇa and the Śrutaprakāśikā, «अयं चार्थः सन्ध्याधिकरणभाष्यश्रुतप्रकाशिकयोः स्पष्टः». He adds that the restriction ‘that alone is the immortal’ excludes the hope that the released and the Supreme are identical, «एतेन अमृतान्तरनिषेधात् मुक्तपरमात्मनोः अभेदप्रत्याशा प्रत्युक्ता».

commentary.q: Madhva: the one awake is Viṣṇu
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: In his comment filed under 2.1.2–3 (see the flags): the individual, who enjoys the fruit of action and sleeps, is the jīva, «यः कर्मफलभोक्ता सुप्त्यादिमान् स जीवः»; he who is awake when beings sleep in dissolution is Viṣṇu, the supreme Brahman, «यः प्रलयादिषु जीवेषु सुप्तेषु जागर्ति स विष्णुः परं ब्रह्मेत्यर्थः».

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Śaṅkara places the scene in dream: the self fashions objects while the senses sleep. Raṅgarāmānuja and Madhva place it at the level of the Lord, awake while all souls sleep, creating by his will (Raṅgarāmānuja) or awake through dissolution (Madhva). For Raṅgarāmānuja the verse rules out identity of the released self with the Supreme; for Śaṅkara it names the one Brahman beside which there is no other.

advaita.text: The self that stays awake through dream is the pure Brahman; there is no other, «तदेव शुक्रं शुभ्रं शुद्धं तद्ब्रह्म नान्यद्गुह्यं ब्रह्मास्ति».

visistadvaita.text: The Supreme creates by his will while all selves sleep; the restriction ‘that alone is immortal’ excludes identity of the released and the Supreme, «मुक्तपरमात्मनोः अभेदप्रत्याशा प्रत्युक्ता».

dvaita.text: The one awake while beings sleep is Viṣṇu, distinct from the sleeping jīva, «यः प्रलयादिषु जीवेषु सुप्तेषु जागर्ति स विष्णुः परं ब्रह्मेत्यर्थः».

schools.disagreement: Śaṅkara reads the wakeful one as the self in dream, one with Brahman; Raṅgarāmānuja and Madhva as the Lord awake among sleeping souls. Raṅgarāmānuja draws from the verse an argument against the identity of the released self and the Supreme; Madhva the difference of jīva and Viṣṇu.

parallels.note: The verse of the inverted aśvattha tree repeats these lines and the two that follow.
Śaṅkara refers back to 2.1.9 for this line.
In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka the person, striking down the body in sleep, sleepless, looks on the sleeping ones.
In dream, where there are no chariots or roads, he creates them: for he is the maker.

contemporary.text: Every night the mind goes on making scenes and wishes while the senses are shut. The verse asks us to notice the one who is present through that making. This is a reflection, not a claim made by the text.

reflect.beginner: When you dream, who is watching the dream?
reflect.deeper: Is kāmaṃ kāmam better read as ‘desire after desire’ or as ‘willing again and again’? What changes with each?
reflect.practice: On waking tomorrow, before moving, recall one dream image and the sense of having been there to see it.

flags.note: Madhva’s text reads ya eṣu supteṣu for ya eṣa supteṣu (corrections.json); the mūla printed with Raṅgarāmānuja also reads एषु, and he glosses «सर्वेषु सुप्तेषु जीवेषु». The vishvAsa mūla spells tasmiṃl lokāḥ with candrabindu (orthographic).
The sleepers: the senses (Śaṅkara), all selves (Raṅgarāmānuja), beings in dissolution (Madhva); kāmaṃ kāmam: noun or absolutive.
Madhva’s comment on this verse is filed in madhva.json under 2.1.2–3 (see 2.2.6); it is cited here as madhva:2.1.2.
